entities: The La Rance tidal barrage in France - operating since 1966, the grand ancestor of tidal power
MeyGen in Scotland - the world's largest tidal stream array
Hawaii's OTEC plant - proving ocean thermal conversion at 100+ kW scale
The European Marine Energy Centre (EMEC) in Orkney - the field's proving ground
how: Ocean energy comes in three main forms. Tidal power captures the rise and fall of tides - either by damming an estuary and generating as water flows through turbines (tidal range), or by placing turbines directly in fast tidal currents (tidal stream). Wave energy converts the up-and-down motion of surface waves via buoys, oscillating flaps, or overtopping reservoirs. Ocean thermal energy conversion (OTEC) exploits the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water to run a heat engine. All three are predictable and renewable, but all must survive the ocean's corrosive, storm-tossed environment.
name: Ocean Energy Harvesting
principles: Predictability is the ocean's edge: tides are forecastable decades out, unlike wind.
Survivability dominates design: the ocean destroys machines, so robustness beats peak efficiency.
Energy density varies wildly: tidal races concentrate power; open ocean spreads it thin.
Corrosion never sleeps: salt water attacks everything, making materials science half the battle.
Niche first, grid later: remote islands and coastal industry are the viable early markets.

public.i: Tide mills proved ocean energy could do useful work fifteen centuries before the grid.
public.k: Medieval tide mills - documented from the 6th century in Ireland and common around the Atlantic coasts by the Middle Ages - trapped high-tide water behind dams and released it through waterwheels to grind grain. They ran on the moon's schedule, not the miller's. The principle - store tidal water, release through a turbine - is identical to modern tidal-range power stations.
public.srcn: Archaeological and historical records of early tide mills, Ireland and Atlantic Europe.
public.title: Tide Mills: The Medieval Beginning

public.i: Girard's patent marks the moment ocean energy became an inventor's problem rather than a miller's craft.
public.k: In 1799 French engineer Pierre-Simon Girard patented machinery for using wave power, one of the first wave-energy patents on record. The 19th century that followed produced hundreds of wave-motor patents - floats, levers, and pumps of every description. Almost none worked economically, but the patent record shows inventors recognized the ocean's energy long before they could capture it.
public.srcn: 19th-century patent records; wave-energy history surveys.
public.title: The Wave-Motor Patent Boom
Victorian Engineers Eye the Tides
public.k: Victorian engineers in the 1850s-60s - including proposals to harness the Severn's tides - drew up serious tidal-power schemes as Britain's industrial appetite grew. None were built: coal was cheap and the engineering was daunting. The proposals established tidal power as a recurring engineering dream.
public.i: The Victorian proposals put tidal power on the engineering agenda a century before La Rance.
public.srcn: 19th-century engineering journals; Severn tidal proposals.

public.i: D'Arsonval's OTEC concept added heat to the ocean-energy menu - temperature as fuel.
public.k: French physicist Jacques-Arsene d'Arsonval proposed in 1881 using the temperature difference between warm tropical surface water and cold deep water to generate power - ocean thermal energy conversion. The physics was sound but the engineering daunting: the temperature difference is small, so plants must move enormous water volumes. The concept waited fifty years for its first demonstration.
public.srcn: D'Arsonval's 1881 proposal; OTEC history literature.
public.title: D'Arsonval Proposes Ocean Thermal Power
Early OTEC Dreamers
public.k: In the early 1900s, popular science writers and engineers championed OTEC as the tropics' destiny - free power from the sea's heat. The enthusiasm outran the thermodynamics, but it kept d'Arsonval's idea alive through decades when no funding existed. Popular imagination preserved the concept.
public.i: Popular enthusiasm kept OTEC alive through its unfunded decades.
public.srcn: Early 20th-century popular science literature.

public.i: The California wave motors showed inventors kept trying even without a market - persistence as R&D.
public.k: Through the 1910s, California inventors built elaborate wave motors off the Pacific coast - rocking barges, air-compressor floats, and lever systems - hoping to power coastal towns. Newspapers covered each attempt breathlessly. None survived the Pacific's winter storms. The attempts mapped, at great expense, exactly how violent the ocean is.
public.srcn: Early 20th-century newspaper archives; California wave-motor patent records.
public.title: California's Wave Motors: Persistence Against the Pacific

public.i: Claude's plant proved OTEC works - and revealed the parasitic-load problem that still defines it.
public.k: Georges Claude, d'Arsonval's student, built an OTEC plant in Cuba in 1930 that generated 22 kW - but consumed more power pumping water than it produced. The net-negative result was honest and instructive: OTEC's physics works, but the engineering margin is brutally thin. Every OTEC design since has been a battle against Claude's parasitic loads.
public.srcn: Claude's OTEC experiments, 1930; engineering analyses.
public.title: Claude's 1930 OTEC Plant in Cuba
Claude's Second Attempt: Brazil
public.k: Undeterred, Claude built a larger OTEC plant off Brazil in the mid-1930s, aiming for megawatt scale. Storms destroyed the cold-water pipe before it operated. The failure was total but instructive: OTEC's vulnerability was the pipe, not the thermodynamics. The cold-water pipe remains OTEC's hardest component.
public.i: The destroyed pipe identified OTEC's true bottleneck: the cold-water intake.
public.srcn: Claude's Brazil expedition records, 1930s.

public.i: Wartime oceanography mapped the seas' energy - military science as accidental resource survey.
public.k: World War II naval research mapped ocean currents, wave climates, and thermal structure at unprecedented detail - data later mined by ocean-energy pioneers. The Navy's wave forecasting for amphibious landings became civilian wave statistics. Military oceanography accidentally surveyed the resource the energy field would later claim.
public.srcn: US Navy oceanographic histories; WWII wave-forecasting records.
public.title: Wartime Oceanography Maps the Resource

public.i: La Rance proved tidal power works at grid scale for sixty years - the field's bedrock reference.
public.k: France's La Rance tidal barrage, completed in 1966 across the Rance estuary in Brittany, installed 240 MW of reversible turbines - still among the largest tidal stations in the world. It has generated reliably for nearly sixty years, with marine life adapting to the basin. La Rance proved tidal range power is a mature, long-lived technology where geography cooperates.
public.srcn: EDF La Rance operating history; tidal-power engineering literature.
public.title: La Rance: The Tidal Barrage That Never Stopped
Kislaya Guba: Russia's Tidal Experiment
public.k: The Soviet Union built the Kislaya Guba tidal station on the Barents Sea in 1968 - a 1.7 MW experimental plant using an innovative floating caisson construction method. It proved tidal plants could be built with prefabricated floating structures. The station operated for decades as a research facility.
public.i: Kislaya Guba pioneered floating construction for tidal plants.
public.srcn: Russian tidal energy records; Kislaya Guba operating history.

public.i: The oil crisis funded ocean energy's first serious R&D wave - and Salter's duck became its icon.
public.k: The 1970s oil shocks poured funding into alternative energy, and Britain's Stephen Salter developed the nodding duck - a cam-shaped float that absorbed wave energy with remarkable efficiency in tank tests. The UK wave program produced brilliant prototypes and honest cost estimates that sobered policymakers. The duck never reached commercial seas, but its lessons shaped every wave device after.
public.srcn: UK wave-energy program records; Salter's duck test reports, 1970s.
public.title: Salter's Duck and the 1970s Wave Program

public.i: OTEC's second wave proved the plants could run - and quantified exactly why they struggle economically.
public.k: The US, Japan, and others funded OTEC research through the 1970s-80s: Hawaii's Mini-OTEC (1979) produced net power, and a 1980s Japanese plant desalinated water as a co-product. The plants worked, but capital costs per kilowatt were enormous and net output modest. OTEC survived as a niche for tropical islands needing both power and fresh water.
public.srcn: US DOE OTEC program reports; Mini-OTEC results, 1979.
public.title: Mini-OTEC: Net Power from the Sea

public.i: Norway's wave experiments proved the ocean breaks machines faster than budgets expect.
public.k: Norway built pioneering wave-power prototypes in the 1980s - the tapered-channel Tapchan and oscillating-water-column plants at Toftestallen. A storm destroyed one; economics sank the other. The Norwegian experience became the field's cautionary tale: the ocean's hundred-year wave, not the average wave, sizes the structure. Survival engineering became the discipline.
public.srcn: Norwegian wave-energy program records, 1980s.
public.title: Norway's Wave Pioneers and the Storm Lesson

public.i: The oscillating water column found wave energy's simplest machine: a concrete box that breathes.
public.k: Through the 1990s, oscillating-water-column plants - like the Pico plant in the Azores and LIMPET on Scotland's Isle of Islay - proved a simple concept: waves compress air in a chamber, driving a turbine. LIMPET fed power to the UK grid from 2000. The OWC's virtue was robustness: concrete and a turbine, with no moving parts in the water.
public.srcn: LIMPET operating reports; Pico plant records.
public.title: Oscillating Water Columns: Concrete That Breathes

public.i: Tidal stream turbines brought wind-turbine thinking underwater - and it worked.
public.k: Engineers realized fast tidal currents could drive underwater turbines much like wind drives windmills, without dams: Marine Current Turbines' SeaGen installed a 1.2 MW tidal-stream turbine in Northern Ireland's Strangford Lough in 2008. It generated reliably for years. The tidal-stream concept - modular, no barrage - opened sites worldwide that could never host a La Rance.
public.srcn: SeaGen operating reports; marine-energy industry histories.
public.title: SeaGen: Turbines in the Tidal Race

public.i: EMEC gave the industry a shared test site - the proving ground every marine technology needed.
public.k: The European Marine Energy Centre opened in Orkney, Scotland in 2003, offering grid-connected wave and tidal test berths with full environmental monitoring. Device developers from around the world queued for berths. EMEC standardized testing, produced comparable performance data, and became the field's de facto certification ground.
public.srcn: EMEC founding records and test program histories.
public.title: EMEC Opens: The Proving Ground

public.i: Pelamis proved wave energy could generate at sea - and that survival economics dominate the field.
public.k: Scotland's Pelamis - a hinged sea-snake of floating segments - generated wave power at the European Marine Energy Centre through the 2000s, the first grid-connected wave farm effort. The company folded in 2014 after struggling with costs and storm damage. Pelamis proved generation works and survivability pays: the ocean breaks machines faster than engineers expect.
public.srcn: EMEC test records; Pelamis company history.
public.title: Pelamis: The Sea Snake

public.i: The Severn debate showed tidal range's political limit: the best sites are also the most contested.
public.k: The UK spent years studying a Severn estuary tidal barrage - potentially 8 GW - through 2008-2012, before shelving it over cost and environmental concerns about the estuary's protected habitats. The Severn saga taught the field that tidal range's constraint is political as much as technical: the biggest tides flow through the most protected waters.
public.srcn: UK Severn Tidal Power feasibility studies.
public.title: The Severn Barrage Debate

public.i: MeyGen proved tidal-stream arrays scale by replication - the wind industry's lesson, applied underwater.
public.k: Scotland's MeyGen project in the Pentland Firth began installing tidal-stream turbines in 2016, growing into the world's largest tidal array at several megawatts, with long-term power purchase contracts. The turbines generated predictably through brutal conditions. MeyGen proved the array model: install, learn, replicate - the path from megawatts to hundreds of megawatts.
public.srcn: MeyGen operating disclosures; SAE Renewables reports.
public.title: MeyGen: The World's Largest Tidal Array
Tidal Stream Goes Multi-Megawatt
public.k: Through 2016-2018, tidal-stream projects multiplied: MeyGen's expansion phases, OpenHydro's testing at EMEC and Fundy, and Tocardo's turbines in the Netherlands. OpenHydro's Fundy turbine was lost in 2018, a costly reminder of the ocean's violence. The survivors consolidated the industry's hard-won knowledge.
public.i: The multi-megawatt phase separated survivors from casualties - consolidation followed.
public.srcn: Industry deployment records, 2016-2018.

public.i: South Korea's Sihwa proved tidal range still scales where the geography is right.
public.k: South Korea's Sihwa Lake tidal power station (254 MW, completed 2011) became the world's largest tidal-range plant, generating predictably in a country with extreme tidal ranges. Its success - built on an existing seawall - showed tidal range remains viable as infrastructure piggybacking, not just greenfield barrages.
public.srcn: Korea Water Resources Corporation operating data.
public.title: Sihwa: Tidal Range at 254 MW

public.i: Hawaii's 105 kW OTEC plant proved continuous ocean-thermal power with valuable co-products.
public.k: Makai Ocean Engineering's OTEC plant in Hawaii, connected in 2015, produced 105 kW of continuous power from the ocean's thermal gradient - the largest US OTEC facility. Its deep cold water also supported aquaculture and air conditioning. The plant proved OTEC's co-product model: power plus water plus cooling can make the economics work where power alone cannot.
public.srcn: Makai Ocean Engineering OTEC reports, 2015.
public.title: Hawaii's OTEC Plant Goes Live

public.i: Second-generation wave devices traded peak efficiency for storm survival - the field's mature engineering judgment.
public.k: Wave developers in the 2010s-20s - CorPower, CalWave, AW-Energy and others - designed devices that detune or submerge in storms, prioritizing survival over maximum energy capture. Tank tests and ocean deployments showed improved reliability. The field's design philosophy had matured: first survive, then optimize.
public.srcn: Company test reports; EMEC and US DOE marine-energy program results.
public.title: Wave Energy's Survival-First Generation

public.i: Orbital's floating turbine proved tidal stream could go where foundations cannot.
public.k: Orbital Marine Power's SR2000 - a 2 MW floating tidal turbine - generated over 3 GWh at EMEC through 2018, proving the floating platform concept. Floating installation slashed deployment costs versus seabed-mounted structures. The SR2000 became the template for the next generation of tidal machines.
public.srcn: Orbital Marine Power test reports, 2018.
public.title: Orbital's Floating Tidal Turbine

public.i: OTEC's island niche proved commercially real: power, water, and cooling from one pipe.
public.k: Through the 2020s, OTEC developers targeted tropical islands and coastal industry where electricity is expensive and fresh water scarce - the economics that favor OTEC's co-products. Projects advanced in Martinique, the Maldives, and Pacific islands. The niche-first strategy accepted OTEC's limits and built a real market inside them.
public.srcn: OTEC project announcements and island-utility studies, 2020s.
public.title: OTEC Finds Its Niche: Islands and Industry

public.i: Nova Scotia's FORCE berth gave North America its tidal test site.
public.k: Canada's Fundy Ocean Research Center for Energy (FORCE) in the Bay of Fundy - home of the world's highest tides - hosted tidal-turbine deployments through 2021, testing devices in 16-meter tidal ranges. The extreme site produced world-class data on turbine performance and environmental interaction. Fundy proved North America had world-class tidal resources.
public.srcn: FORCE berth reports; Bay of Fundy turbine deployments.
public.title: Fundy: Testing in the World's Highest Tides

public.i: Tidal stream reached cost-competitive territory in the best races - the learning curve working underwater.
public.k: By 2022-2024, tidal-stream operators reported capacity factors above 40 percent in prime races and levelized costs falling toward offshore wind's early levels, with larger rotors and array experience driving gains. The UK's contract-for-difference rounds began including tidal stream. The technology crossed from demonstration to deployable in the world's best tidal sites.
public.srcn: UK CfD allocation rounds; tidal industry cost reports, 2022-2024.
public.title: Tidal Stream's Cost Curve Bends

public.i: CorPower's C4 proved wave energy could survive storms and generate - both at once.
public.k: Sweden's CorPower Ocean deployed its C4 wave device off Portugal in 2023, demonstrating storm survival through detuning plus strong generation in normal seas. The device's phase-control technology boosted energy capture significantly. C4 became wave energy's most credible proof that survival and performance can coexist.
public.srcn: CorPower Ocean deployment reports, 2023.
public.title: CorPower C4: Surviving and Generating
Wave Energy's Funding Returns
public.k: In 2024, wave energy attracted renewed investment - the US DOE's prize programs, EU funding rounds, and private capital returning to survivors like CorPower. The funding thesis had matured: back devices with ocean survival data, not just tank tests. Capital discipline replaced the 2000s exuberance.
public.i: Disciplined capital returned to wave energy's proven survivors.
public.srcn: DOE and EU marine-energy funding announcements, 2024.

public.i: Floating tidal and hybrid platforms expanded the addressable ocean - no seabed foundation required.
public.k: Developers deployed floating tidal-stream platforms and hybrid wind-wave systems through 2024-2025, cutting installation costs by avoiding seabed foundations. The floating approach opened deeper, faster waters to tidal development. Hybrid platforms sharing moorings and cables between wind and wave improved project economics.
public.srcn: Company deployment announcements, 2024-2025.
public.title: Floating Platforms and Hybrids

public.i: Tidal lagoons returned as the barrage's gentler successor - impoundment without damming an estuary.
public.k: Through 2025, developers advanced tidal-lagoon proposals - artificial impoundments in shallow coastal water that generate on the tide without blocking a river. The lagoon concept keeps La Rance's reliability while sidestepping the estuary politics that killed the Severn. Welsh and French projects moved through permitting.
public.srcn: Tidal lagoon project proposals and permitting records, 2025.
public.title: Tidal Lagoons: The Barrage's Successor
Salinity Gradient: The Fourth Ocean Energy
public.k: Through 2025, salinity-gradient power - generating electricity from the difference between salt and fresh water at river mouths - advanced from lab to pilot, with new membrane technologies improving on earlier prototypes. The resource is enormous where rivers meet the sea. It remains pre-commercial but represents the ocean's fourth energy form.
public.i: Salinity gradient added a fourth harvestable ocean energy form.
public.srcn: Salinity-gradient research literature; pilot announcements.

public.i: The working version is real but bounded: ocean energy serves its niches superbly and the open ocean remains a frontier.
public.k: By 2025-2026, ocean energy harvesting had reached a working version with clear boundaries: tidal-range barrages generate reliably where built, tidal-stream arrays operate commercially in prime races, OTEC serves tropical island niches, and wave energy remains pre-commercial but improving. Total global capacity is small beside wind and solar, but in its niches - predictable power for coastal grids and islands - the ocean delivers.
public.srcn: IEA Ocean Energy Systems reports 2025-2026; industry capacity statistics.
public.title: The Working Version: Ocean Energy Today

short: Technologies that generate electricity from tides, waves, and ocean temperature differences.

signature.i: The oldest machine is often the clearest teacher; the Signature system studies first principles in old iron.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of tide mills emphasizes first principles: store water at height, release through a machine. Fifteen centuries of refinement changed the machine from wood to steel but not the principle. Signature methodology holds that technologies whose principles never change are the most trustworthy - the physics was settled before the industry existed.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Fifteen Centuries of the Same Principle

signature.i: Patent counts are an innovation metric; the Signature system reads them as enthusiasm data.
signature.k: The Signature analysis treats the 19th-century wave-motor patent boom as enthusiasm data: hundreds of patents, near-zero deployments. Signature innovation metrics discount patent counts without deployment - enthusiasm is not progress. The boom's real value was mapping the design space's dead ends.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Patents as Enthusiasm Data
Signature Reading: The Recurring Dream
signature.k: The Signature analysis treats tidal power's Victorian proposals as a recurring dream - an idea that resurfaces whenever energy prices spike. Signature innovation theory holds that recurring dreams signal a real resource waiting for enabling technology. Tidal power recurred for a century before La Rance proved it.
signature.i: Recurring dreams mark real resources awaiting enabling technology.
Thin-margin physics demands honest engineering; the Signature system respects technologies that admit it.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of d'Arsonval's concept emphasizes the thin margin: small temperature differences mean enormous water flows, and the physics cannot be negotiated. Signature doctrine holds that thin-margin technologies must be engineered with exceptional honesty - every parasitic load accounted. OTEC's history is a seminar in margin discipline.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Thin Margin
Signature Reading: Imagination as Preservation
signature.k: The Signature treatment values popular enthusiasm as concept preservation: when no funding exists, imagination keeps ideas alive. Signature methodology holds that unfunded decades are survivable if the concept stays in circulation. OTEC survived on imagination until the 1970s funded it.
signature.i: Imagination preserves concepts through unfunded decades.
The ocean grades on survival; the Signature system designs for the hundred-year wave.
signature.k: The Signature analysis of California's wave motors extracts the survival lesson: the Pacific destroyed every device, teaching that the design load is the storm, not the average. Signature engineering sizes structures for the extreme event - the hundred-year wave - and treats average conditions as the economic case. Survivability first is not caution; it is arithmetic.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Designed for the Storm

signature.i: Net-negative results are data; the Signature system values honest failure above optimistic modeling.
signature.k: The Signature treatment honors Claude's net-negative plant: he published the parasitic loads instead of hiding them. Signature doctrine holds that honest negative results advance a field more than optimistic models - Claude's numbers defined OTEC's real problem for a century. The 22 kW that cost more than it made taught everything.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Honest Negative
Signature Reading: Finding the Real Bottleneck
signature.k: The Signature analysis of Claude's destroyed pipe extracts the bottleneck discipline: the failure identified the cold-water pipe, not the heat engine, as OTEC's true hard problem. Signature engineering always asks which component actually fails - the answer redirects R&D spending. The pipe, not the turbine, deserved the budget.
signature.i: Failures identify the true bottleneck; budgets should follow.
Military science is an accidental R&D subsidy; the Signature system mines it deliberately.
signature.k: The Signature analysis treats WWII oceanography as an accidental resource survey: naval research mapped the energy field's raw material for free. Signature scouting systematically mines military science for civilian applications - the data is public, the instruments were expensive, and the mapping is done. Ocean energy inherited the Navy's charts.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Accidental Survey

signature.i: Sixty-year machines are the gold standard; the Signature system trusts what outlives its builders.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of La Rance emphasizes longevity as the ultimate proof: nearly sixty years of generation outlasts every projection model. Signature reliability doctrine holds that the best evidence for a technology is a machine still running decades after commissioning. La Rance is the field's existence proof that tidal power endures.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Sixty-Year Machine
Signature Reading: Construction Innovation
signature.k: The Signature treatment of Kislaya Guba highlights construction method as innovation: floating caissons made tidal plants buildable. Signature doctrine holds that construction innovation often matters more than device innovation - the machine is only half the project. The Soviets innovated the building, not the turbine.
signature.i: Construction methods are half the technology.
Beautiful prototypes that never deploy are still valuable; the Signature system banks their lessons.
signature.k: The Signature analysis values Salter's duck despite its non-deployment: the tank tests, efficiency measurements, and cost estimates became the field's shared knowledge. Signature methodology holds that brilliant failures are R&D assets - the duck's data informed every later device. Non-deployment is not the same as worthlessness.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Valuable Non-Deployment

signature.i: Co-products rescue thin margins; the Signature system designs for them deliberately.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of Mini-OTEC emphasizes the co-product insight: power alone could not pay, but power plus water plus cooling could. Signature economics holds that thin-margin technologies must stack revenue streams - the single-product business case is the trap. OTEC's survival came from selling three things, not one.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Stacking Revenue Streams

signature.i: The ocean is the strictest teacher; the Signature system enrolls every technology in its school.
signature.k: The Signature analysis of Norway's destroyed prototypes treats the storm losses as tuition: the ocean taught, at great expense, that survival engineering is the discipline. Signature methodology holds that harsh environments are the best validators - a device that survives the Norwegian Sea will survive anywhere. The tuition was worth paying.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Tuition Paid to the Sea

signature.i: Simplicity is a survival strategy; the Signature system favors the concrete box over the clever machine.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of the oscillating water column celebrates radical simplicity: concrete, air, and a turbine - nothing fragile in the water. Signature design doctrine holds that in hostile environments, the simplest adequate machine wins. LIMPET's longevity vindicated the concrete box.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Concrete Box Wins

signature.i: Crossover thinking - wind turbines underwater - is the Signature system's favorite move.
signature.k: The Signature analysis treats tidal-stream turbines as technology crossover: wind-turbine knowledge applied underwater, skipping decades of independent development. Signature scouting hunts such crossovers - the best solution to your problem may be mature in another industry. SeaGen was wind energy's underwater second act.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Wind's Underwater Second Act

signature.i: Shared test sites are industry infrastructure; the Signature system funds them as public goods.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of EMEC emphasizes the test-site model: shared berths, standardized measurements, and comparable data accelerated the whole field. Signature industrial policy holds that test infrastructure is a public good - no single startup can afford what the industry needs collectively. EMEC was the field's laboratory.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Shared Laboratory

signature.i: Elegant failures teach elegantly; the Signature system studies them closely.
signature.k: The Signature analysis of Pelamis is respectful: the sea snake was beautiful, innovative, and ultimately uneconomic - and its failure taught the field more than a modest success would have. Signature methodology holds that ambitious failures map the boundary of the possible. Pelamis drew the map.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Elegant Failure

signature.i: Political constraints are engineering constraints; the Signature system designs around them.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of the Severn saga emphasizes the political binding constraint: the best technical site was undevelopable for environmental reasons. Signature project doctrine holds that political feasibility is a design input, not an afterthought - the Severn's lesson redirected the field toward lagoons and streams. Politics is part of the physics.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Politics as Physics

signature.i: Replication is the scaling strategy; the Signature system distrusts bespoke megaprojects.
signature.k: The Signature analysis of MeyGen emphasizes the array model: identical turbines, installed in sequence, each cheaper than the last. Signature manufacturing doctrine holds that replication beats enlargement - the tenth turbine teaches what the first could not. MeyGen proved the ocean industry could learn like the wind industry.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Array Model

signature.i: Infrastructure piggybacking is the cheapest deployment; the Signature system looks for existing structures.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of Sihwa highlights the piggyback: an existing seawall became a power station's foundation. Signature deployment doctrine hunts such piggybacks - infrastructure built for one purpose serving another. The cheapest megawatt is the one that reuses concrete.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Piggyback Principle

signature.i: Co-products are the business model; the Signature system never evaluates thin-margin tech on one revenue stream.
signature.k: The Signature analysis of Hawaii's OTEC plant centers the co-product stack: power, aquaculture, cooling - three revenues from one pipe. Signature economics requires stacked revenues for thin-margin technologies. The plant's lesson is general: sell everything the process produces.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Sell Everything

signature.i: Mature judgment looks like pessimism; the Signature system recognizes it as wisdom.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of wave energy's survival-first turn respects the field's mature judgment: after decades of destroyed devices, prioritizing survival over efficiency was wisdom, not timidity. Signature engineering holds that hard-won conservatism is an asset - the field finally designed for the ocean it has, not the ocean it wishes for.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Wisdom Looks Like Caution

signature.i: Floating anything is cheaper than founding anything; the Signature system floats first.
signature.k: The Signature analysis of Orbital's floating turbine emphasizes the installation economics: floating platforms avoid the costliest marine operation - seabed foundations. Signature deployment doctrine prefers floating where physics allows. The ocean's surface is cheaper real estate than its floor.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Float First

signature.i: Niches are not consolation prizes; the Signature system treats them as beachheads.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of OTEC's island niche rejects the consolation-prize framing: islands with expensive power and scarce water are a genuine market, not a retreat. Signature market strategy holds that beachheads fund the march inland - or in this case, outward. The niche is the business.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Beachhead Niche

signature.i: Extreme sites produce extreme data; the Signature system values the harshest test.
signature.k: The Signature analysis of Fundy's 16-meter tides treats the extreme site as the ultimate validator: devices proven in the world's highest tides carry credibility everywhere. Signature testing doctrine seeks the harshest representative environment - passing there de-risks everywhere else. Fundy is the ocean-energy SAT.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Ultimate Validator

signature.i: Learning curves work underwater; the Signature system trusts the replication math.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of tidal stream's cost decline applies the learning-curve faith: each doubling of installed capacity cuts costs, underwater as on land. Signature forecasting holds that manufactured technologies follow the curve regardless of medium. The ocean is not exempt from economics.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Curve Holds Underwater
Signature Reading: Consolidation as Progress
signature.k: The Signature analysis treats the tidal industry's consolidation as healthy: lost turbines and the survivors' gains concentrated knowledge in viable designs. Signature industrial theory holds that shakeouts are information - the market selecting the designs that survive the ocean. Consolidation is the field maturing.
signature.i: Shakeouts concentrate knowledge in surviving designs.
Survival plus performance is the combination that matters; the Signature system waited decades for it.
signature.k: The Signature analysis marks CorPower's C4 as the combination event: storm survival and strong generation in one device. Signature evaluation holds that single-attribute successes prove little - the field needed both at once. C4 delivered the combination the industry had chased since Salter's duck.
signature.title: Signature Reading: The Combination Event

signature.i: Shared moorings, shared cables, shared costs; the Signature system shares infrastructure.
signature.k: The Signature treatment of hybrid platforms emphasizes infrastructure sharing: one mooring system, one cable, two energy sources. Signature project economics holds that shared infrastructure is the fastest cost reduction available. The hybrid's math is simple: divide the fixed costs by two.
signature.title: Signature Reading: Divide the Fixed Costs
Signature Reading: Disciplined Capital
signature.k: The Signature treatment of wave energy's funding return emphasizes the discipline: capital now demands ocean survival data before investing. Signature finance doctrine holds that disciplined capital accelerates real technologies and starves fantasies. The 2024 funding was smarter money than the 2000s money.
signature.i: Disciplined capital is a technology's best investor.
The gentler successor often wins; the Signature system watches for the redesign that keeps the virtue and drops the vice.
signature.k: The Signature analysis of tidal lagoons sees the classic successor pattern: keep La Rance's reliability, drop the estuary conflict. Signature innovation theory holds that many breakthroughs are subtractions - removing the objectionable part while preserving the working part. The lagoon is the barrage minus the politics.

signature.i: The Signature projection: predictable power becomes the ocean's premium product as grids go renewable.
signature.k: The Signature forward projection for ocean energy sees its value rising as grids decarbonize: predictable tidal power commands a premium in systems dominated by variable wind and solar. The projection models tidal stream reaching hundreds of megawatts by the mid-2030s, wave energy crossing to commercial in sheltered markets, and OTEC standardizing for island utilities. This is Signature projection, clearly labeled: the predictability premium is real, the deployment timeline is modeled.
signature.title: Signature Projection: The Predictability Premium

status_note: Emerging - tidal stream arrays operate commercially in prime sites; tidal range is established where built; wave energy remains pre-commercial; OTEC serves island niches. Total capacity is small but growing.
what: Ocean energy harvesting is the set of technologies that generate electricity from the sea: tides (both the rise-and-fall range and fast tidal currents), surface waves, and the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water. It matters because the ocean's energy is vast, renewable, and - in the case of tides - perfectly predictable decades in advance, a quality no other renewable offers.
why: As grids decarbonize, predictable clean power becomes increasingly valuable: wind and solar are cheap but variable, while tides arrive on schedule. Coastal nations and island communities - often dependent on expensive imported diesel - are the natural first markets. The technologies have matured from Victorian wave motors to commercial tidal arrays, though the ocean remains the harshest engineering environment on Earth.
